blocks.text: An **attitude** is a **learned, relatively enduring evaluative disposition** — favourable or unfavourable — toward an object, person, idea or institution. Its **content/structure** is the **ABC (tri-component) model**: **A**ffective (feelings — 'I like the office of the collector'), **B**ehavioural (action tendency — 'I will prepare for Group-I'), **C**ognitive (beliefs — 'the civil service enables large-scale good'). Attitudes vary on **valence** (direction), **extremity/strength**, **accessibility** (how fast they activate), **explicit vs implicit** (professed vs automatic — implicit caste/gender bias can contradict professed equality: crucial administrative insight).

sections.heading: Attitude ↔ thought and behaviour — the honest relationship

items: **Attitudes influence thought**: they filter attention and memory (**confirmation bias**) — an officer convinced 'beneficiaries cheat' will find cheating and miss exclusion errors.

**But behaviour doesn't follow automatically** — **LaPiere (1934)** (Chinese couple served despite anti-Chinese attitudes) showed the attitude-behaviour gap; behaviour follows best when the attitude is **strong, specific, personally experienced and socially supported** (Fishbein-Ajzen's **theory of planned behaviour**: intention = attitude + subjective norms + perceived control).

**Behaviour also creates attitude**: **cognitive dissonance (Festinger)** — acting against one's attitude generates discomfort resolved by attitude change (officers made to conduct social audits often become audit-believers); **foot-in-the-door** and role-playing effects.

**Administrative payoff**: to change public behaviour (sanitation, helmet use), change **norms and ease of action**, not just minds — the **nudge** insight (SBM's community-led total sanitation worked on norms, not pamphlets).

flowchart TD
  A[Cognition - beliefs] --> D[Attitude]
  B[Affect - feelings] --> D
  C[Behavioural tendency] --> D

items: **Formation**: direct experience (strongest), classical/operant conditioning, **observational learning** (Bandura), group affiliation, media & repetition (mere-exposure effect).

**Change routes — Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo)**: **central route** (quality arguments, when audience is motivated & able — policy consultations) vs **peripheral route** (source attractiveness, emotion, slogans — mass campaigns); durable change needs the central route.

**Persuasion variables**: credible + trustworthy source (why **ASHA/ANM** vaccine messengers beat ads), two-sided messages for educated audiences, moderate fear + efficacy (COVID messaging lesson), inoculation against misinformation.

**AP hook**: attitude-change programmes at scale — **Swachh** behaviour change, e-crop/DBT shifting farmer attitudes toward formal systems, and police 'Disha' app adoption as trust-building — evaluate each as central vs peripheral persuasion.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Definitions + ABC + Katz's four functions + LaPiere/dissonance + ELM is the complete toolkit. In case studies, name the function an attitude is serving (ego-defensive?) and the route you'd use to change it — that vocabulary converts psychology into administration.

prelimsPointers: **ABC model**: Affective, Behavioural, Cognitive components of attitude.
**Katz (1960)**: four functions — utilitarian, knowledge, ego-defensive, value-expressive.
**LaPiere (1934)**: classic demonstration of the attitude–behaviour gap.
**Festinger (1957)**: cognitive dissonance — discomfort from inconsistent cognitions drives attitude change.
**Theory of planned behaviour (Ajzen)**: attitude + subjective norm + perceived behavioural control → intention → behaviour.
**Elaboration Likelihood Model**: central (argument-based, durable) vs peripheral (cue-based, fragile) persuasion.
**Mere-exposure effect (Zajonc)**: repeated exposure alone increases liking.

glossary.definition: A learned, enduring evaluation — positive or negative — of an object, person or idea, predisposing responses toward it.
Psychological tension from holding inconsistent cognitions or acting against one's attitudes, typically resolved by changing the attitude.
Automatic, unconscious evaluation that may diverge from professed views — the seat of unexamined bias.
Attitude change through careful processing of argument quality; produces durable, behaviour-linked attitudes.
Perceived social expectation regarding a behaviour — often the decisive lever in public-behaviour campaigns.
The tendency to seek and weigh evidence that supports existing attitudes while discounting contrary evidence.

blocks.text: A **moral attitude** is an evaluative disposition anchored in **right/wrong judgments** (justice, honesty, care, purity) — experienced as **objective and non-negotiable**, which is why moral disagreements escalate (moral conviction resists compromise, majority pressure and even law). A **political attitude** is a disposition toward **power, institutions and policy** — ideology (left–right; liberty–equality trade-offs), party identification, trust in institutions, and issue positions. The two interlock: **moralised politics** (when policy becomes sacred value) mobilises intensely but polarises dangerously — the administrator must convert moralised conflict back into negotiable interests.

rows: Family & early socialisation, religion, **moral emotions** (guilt, empathy, disgust), Kohlberg-stage reasoning, moral exemplars
Predicts integrity under pressure; source of conscientious objection; also of moral rigidity
Family transmission (strongest single predictor), class/caste/region identity, media ecosystems, generational events (Emergency, liberalisation, bifurcation of AP)
Officer must be **politically aware but politically neutral** — serving all attitudes without sharing any publicly

items: **Haidt's Moral Foundations Theory** — care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity (+liberty): different publics weight foundations differently; policy communication that speaks only 'care/fairness' misses 'loyalty/sanctity' audiences — a persuasion insight for field officers.

**Civil servant's line**: the AIS Conduct Rules bar public political expression; neutrality of conduct need not mean moral neutrality — an officer is partisan for the **Constitution's** morality (equality, dignity, secular fairness) while neutral among **parties**.

sections.heading: Social influence — how attitudes move people

items: **Conformity** — **Asch (1951)**: 1/3 conformed to obviously wrong majorities; drivers: normative (fit in) & informational (they must know) influence; antidote: one dissenter breaks the spell — institutional lesson: protect the first dissenting voice (file notings, board minority notes).

**Obedience** — **Milgram (1963)**: ~65% administered 'maximum shocks' under authority; gradual escalation + diffused responsibility; administrative parallel: illegal orders executed down a chain — hence the rule of **written orders** and personal liability for manifestly illegal commands.
**Compliance techniques**: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-balling — recognise them in vendor negotiations and political demands.

**Group dynamics**: **groupthink (Janis)** — cohesive groups suppress dissent (policy fiascos); **group polarisation** — deliberation among the like-minded radicalises (social-media echo chambers; communal rumour cascades — the DM's first task in tension: break the information monoculture).

**Persuasion in public life**: source credibility, message framing (loss vs gain), narrative > statistics for mass audiences, **prebunking** misinformation — the modern district communication toolkit.

sections.heading: The AP field view and answer craft

items: **Live applications**: rumour-driven mob events and the administrator's counter-speech duty; faction politics of Rayalaseema as inherited political attitudes; welfare-scheme credit wars moralising policy; social-media polarisation around bifurcation-era grievances (SCS) — each is a social-influence case study waiting to be cited.

**Officer's toolkit**: institutionalise dissent (red-team reviews), rotate advisory circles (anti-groupthink), pre-bunk before festivals/verdicts, engage credible local messengers (clergy, SHG leaders, teachers), and keep own political attitudes off the record — **visible neutrality is itself a trust technology**.

blocks.text: Exam tip: This theme = definitions (moral vs political attitude) + Asch/Milgram/Janis with numbers + two administrative safeguards + one AP application. Examiners specifically reward the experiments' figures (1/3, 65%) and the institutional translation.

prelimsPointers: **Asch (1951)**: ~33% conformity to wrong majority judgments; unanimity is the key variable — one dissenter collapses conformity.
**Milgram (1963)**: ~65% obeyed to the maximum shock level; proximity of victim and authority legitimacy moderate obedience.
**Janis (1972)**: groupthink — illusion of unanimity, self-censorship, mindguards; remedy: devil's advocacy.
**Moral Foundations Theory (Haidt)**: care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity, liberty.
**Group polarisation**: post-discussion attitudes become more extreme in the initially favoured direction.
AIS (Conduct) Rules bar public political comment and political-party association for officers.
**Normative vs informational** social influence — Deutsch & Gerard (1955).

glossary.definition: An evaluative disposition grounded in judgments of right and wrong, experienced as objective and resistant to compromise.
Disposition toward power, institutions, parties and policy — shaped by family, identity and formative events.
Adjusting behaviour or belief to group norms under normative or informational influence (Asch).
Compliance with directives of authority — capable of overriding conscience under gradual escalation (Milgram).
Deterioration of judgment in cohesive groups that prize consensus over realistic appraisal (Janis).
Fidelity to the Constitution's values — equality, dignity, due process — as the public servant's operative moral compass, above popular or personal morality.

blocks.text: **Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capacity to **perceive, understand, use and regulate emotions — one's own and others'** — to guide thought and action. Coined by **Salovey & Mayer (1990)** (ability model: perceiving → using → understanding → managing emotions), popularised by **Daniel Goleman (1995)**, whose mixed model gives the exam-standard **five components**: **self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills**. Goleman's claim: for leadership, EI matters about **twice as much as IQ and technical skill combined**; IQ gets you hired, EI gets you followed. Measures: MSCEIT (ability), EQ-i/360° (mixed) — measurement debates make good critical-balance material.

sections.heading: EI in administration and governance — where it bites

items: **Crisis leadership**: disasters demand calm authority + empathy — AP's cyclone-evacuation record is an EI-at-scale story: persuading fishermen ashore is emotional labour before it is logistics.

**Citizen interface**: welfare counters, grievance hearings (Spandana), police stations — **procedural justice research** shows people accept adverse decisions delivered with respect and voice; EI operationalises dignity.
**Team & change management**: transfers, mergers, digitisation resistance — regulation of others' anxiety decides implementation speed; 'people don't resist change, they resist loss'.
**Negotiation & conflict**: land acquisition, inter-departmental turf, communal mediation — empathy maps interests behind positions.

**Ethical guardrail**: self-aware officers catch their biases; self-regulated ones resist anger-driven and fear-driven misjudgment; BUT note the **dark side** — high-EI manipulation (emotional skill serving unethical ends) — EI needs ethics as its rudder.

**Cultivation**: reflective journaling, mindfulness (evidence-backed), 360° feedback, empathy exposure (field immersion — the reason training academies mandate village stays), **Mission Karmayogi's** behavioural-competency frame.

Quote Aristotle: 'Anyone can become angry — that is easy; but to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time — that is not easy.'

**AP examples bank**: cyclone evacuations (Hudhud → zero-casualty doctrine), Spandana grievance hearings, land-pooling negotiation for Amaravati (consent of ~34,000 acres' farmers — a masterclass in interest-based persuasion, whatever its later politics), tribal-area service delivery needing cultural empathy.

blocks.text: Exam tip: EI questions are application questions in disguise — every mark lies in the administrative translation column. Prepare one crisis, one counter-service and one negotiation example from AP and reuse them across EI, attitude and leadership questions.

prelimsPointers: EI term coined by **Salovey & Mayer (1990)**; four-branch ability model.
**Goleman (1995)**: *Emotional Intelligence — Why It Can Matter More Than IQ*; five components; later four-domain leadership model.
**EQ vs IQ**: Goleman's leadership research attributes the majority of star-performance variance to EI competencies.
**MSCEIT** measures ability EI; **EQ-i (Bar-On)** measures trait/mixed EI.
**Amygdala hijack** — Goleman's term for emotion overwhelming rational response; regulation restores prefrontal control.
**Mission Karmayogi (2020)** embeds behavioural competencies (including EI) in civil-service capability frameworks.
Procedural-justice research (**Tyler**): perceived fairness of process drives acceptance of outcomes.

glossary.definition: The ability to perceive, understand, use and manage emotions in oneself and others to guide effective thought and action.
Managing disruptive impulses and moods — composure, adaptability and considered response under pressure.
Accurately sensing and considering others' emotions and perspectives — cognitive, emotional and compassionate variants.
A rapid, overwhelming emotional reaction that bypasses deliberative brain circuits — the failure mode self-regulation prevents.
Managing one's displayed emotions as part of a work role — the unacknowledged workload of frontline public servants.
Fairness of decision processes (voice, neutrality, respect, trustworthiness) — the strongest predictor of citizen acceptance of authority.
